scenes.title: Watch the steady climb
scenes.source: Recording93–110 main inclined-car example, original values

beats.text: Consider a vehicle climbing a straight, shallow hill. Its engine keeps it moving uphill at a steady speed. Watch the wheels and the roadside markers: equal distances pass in equal times.
The engine drives uphill. Resistance opposes the motion, and gravity also pulls back down the slope. The vehicle keeps climbing without gaining speed.
We want the engine power needed for this steady climb. First, let us put the whole question on the diagram.

scenes.title: The complete question

beats.text: The vehicle has a mass of one thousand kilograms and moves uphill on a straight road.
The road makes angle theta with the horizontal, with sine theta equal to one over twenty. This really is a very shallow slope.
Its speed is a steady twenty metres per second, uphill.
Call the non gravitational resistance f. It is a constant five hundred newtons downhill, opposite the motion.
Take g as ten metres per second squared. Model the vehicle as a particle.
The engine driving force D acts uphill, parallel to the motion. The road reaction is perpendicular to the road.
Find the engine power P in kilowatts. The driving force is also unknown. All our givens are here. Pause before we start calculating.

scenes.title: How quickly is work being done?

beats.text: Power tells us how quickly work is done. Average power over a time interval equals the work done divided by the elapsed time.
Here W means work in joules, while power is measured in watts. A watt means a joule per second.
Now consider a constant driving force D, parallel to motion, at constant speed. Over distance s, its work is force times distance.
Divide that work by the time. Distance divided by time is the constant speed v. So power equals driving force times speed.
When speed changes, D times v still gives the instantaneous power of a parallel driving force. Use the force and speed at that same instant, not the average speed of a whole journey.
beats.caption: Same instant · force parallel to motion

scenes.title: First find the driving force
scenes.source: Recording109–148; PDF4 force diagram and balance

beats.text: Steady speed along a straight road means zero acceleration. We use a snapshot to analyse the forces; the real vehicle is still moving.
Take uphill as positive. Replace weight by its components. Only m g sine theta acts along the road, downhill. Reaction is perpendicular, so it does not enter this uphill balance.
beats.caption: Along the slope · uphill positive

beats.text: Start with Newton’s second law: resultant force equals mass times acceleration. Along the road, driving force minus resistance f minus the weight component equals m a, which is zero.
Substitute resistance five hundred, mass one thousand, g ten, and sine theta one over twenty. Keep the driving force as D.
Mass times g times sine theta gives five hundred newtons down the slope.
Move both opposing forces to the other side. The engine driving force is one thousand newtons uphill.
The engine force balances the two downhill contributions. Zero resultant force does not mean zero driving force. This is why the vehicle can keep climbing at steady speed.

scenes.title: Then calculate the engine power

beats.text: We now know the driving force. It is parallel to the uphill velocity, so engine power equals driving force times speed.
Use the engine force of one thousand newtons and the speed of twenty metres per second. Do not put the zero resultant force into this engine power formula.
The engine power is twenty thousand watts.
The question asks for kilowatts. One kilowatt is one thousand watts.
Divide twenty thousand by one thousand. The required engine power is twenty kilowatts.
That power supplies work continually as the vehicle climbs against gravity and resistance. A constant speed does not mean that the engine has stopped doing work.

scenes.title: What changes at constant power?

beats.text: Now change the condition: hold engine power constant, and compare two nonzero speeds. We are comparing moving snapshots, not modelling a launch from rest.
Start from power equals driving force times speed. Rearrange it: driving force equals power divided by speed.

At the same power, a higher speed leaves a smaller driving force. The shorter arrow shows that change. A vehicle using maximum power reaches its limiting steady speed when the driving force balances all opposing forces.
beats.caption: Same power · higher speed · smaller force

beats.text: Return to our steady climb. Since the resultant force is zero, must the engine power be zero? Think about which force belongs in the formula.
beats.caption: Zero resultant: zero engine power?

beats.text: No. Use the engine driving force, not the resultant. The engine still does positive work while gravity and resistance oppose the climb.
beats.caption: Engine power uses the driving force
